title: Attention quantum jitter scan
content:
TL;DR: Running a focused sweep of small, intermittent latency spikes that appear when switching between FlashAttention and paged-attn execution paths. Goal is to capture micro-jitter characteristics (distribution, trigger signals, sequence-length dependence) and produce reproducible microbenchmarks and mitigations.

Background / Why this doc:
- Over the past 3 weeks we saw sporadic P95->P99 jumps in downstream request latency on mixed-traffic clusters. Patterns: short bursts (~100–300ms extra tail for generation calls), often correlated with sequence length transitions and sometimes after KV-cache warmups.
- Hypothesis space: (A) kernel handoff jitter (kernel selection + priming), (B) memory thrash + prefetch fallthrough when FlashAttention falls back to paged paths, (C) fused-op ordering interaction causing register pressure spikes, (D) scheduling/backpressure ripple in coalescer that surfaces as jitter.
- This notebook-style log captures the experiments we've run and results so far, command lines, quick plots (text summary), and next steps. Intend to convert to a reproducible bench harness once we lock the key signals.

Setup notes (env):
- GPU: A100-40GB, cuda 12.1, cudnn 9.1, driver 535.x
- Runtime build: main@2024-11-01 + experimental prefetched-kernel-switch flag (see PR 842)
- Models tested: small transformer toy (8-layer, 512 hidden, 8 heads) + Llama-like 7B checkpoint (quantized int8 eager path)
- Traffic: synthetic client sending interleaved short (prompt len 8) & long (prompt len 256) requests to mimic PLG patterns
- Measurement harness: per-request wall clock around runtime invoke, internal telemetry: kernel_choice, cache_hit_rate, batch_size, kernel_latency_ns (per-op), host->device memcpy time.

Experiment A: deterministic sequence-length jitter scan
- Procedure: 1) Warm the model with 1000 short requests; 2) Send 500 alternating short/long sequences at 50 RPS; 3) Toggle the kernel switch policy: aggressive-flash (prefer flash if compatible) vs conservative (prefer paged) vs dynamic (current shipping).
- Observations: aggressive-flash reduced median by ~6% but increased P99 by ~22% (for multi-tenant load). Conservative reduced P99 slightly but raised median by ~12%. Dynamic showed intermittent spikes matching times when the sequence length changes caused a kernel-switch event.
- Logged signal correlation: kernel_choice change events align w/ jitter events in ~78% of spikes; memcpy peaks precede 64% of spikes by ~3–7ms.

Experiment B: prefetch hysteresis stress
- Procedure: stress cluster with repeated long-tail requests while manipulating prefetch hysteresis thresholds on the FlashPaged path.
- Observations: lowering hysteresis reduces how often Flash attempts a risky prefetch -> fewer fallback events, but increased average op latency during warmups. When hysteresis is too permissive we see rapid prefetch->fallback cycles that produce 200–400ms spikes as memory paths reconfigure.

Microbench results (summary numbers):
- Toy model, 1-request-per-batch stream, median latency: flash=26ms, paged=31ms. P99: flash=82ms, paged=61ms.
- Llama-7B (int8 path), mixed load: median flash=87ms, paged=98ms. P99 flash=412ms, paged=173ms. NOTE: large P99 on flash correlates with fallback events and memcpy surges.

Preliminary root-cause synthesis:
- Primary contributor appears to be kernel handoff + priming cost when switching from a paged/prefetch-safe context into FlashAttention or vice versa. The runtime currently performs a micro-priming sequence (allocs, kernel selection, KV-layout adjustments) that is fast in isolation but when coupled with device memcpy/backpressure and fused-op register pressure, becomes amplified in the P99 region.
- Secondary contributor is prefetch hysteresis oscillation where an optimistic prefetch triggers fallback due to transient memory pressure; the fallback path runs a different fused-op ordering causing temporary register thrash and longer kernels.

Repro case recipe (for infra team):
1) Checkout serving-runtime@pr/842 (link above).
2) Build with KERN_SWITCH_LOG=1 and PREFETCH_HYSTERESIS=0.12.
3) Launch single-node A100 with 12 worker threads. 1 client process using rps-client v0.3 to generate the alternating sequences (config attached in linked artifact).
4) Capture /tmp/attn-quantum-*.log (we emit kernel_choice timestamps + memcpy histograms) and the OS slab and gpu-memory statistics every 50ms (nvidia-smi stats).

Quick mitigations to test (short list):
- Add a lightweight kernel-priming fast-path that pre-initializes kernels for the 2 most-likely sequence-length bands (e.g., [<32], [32–256]) to eliminate alloc+setup on first hit.
- Extend prefetch hysteresis with a simple cooldown window (300ms) to avoid flipflop prefetch->fallback cycles under bursty multi-tenant traffic.
- Prefer asynchronous memcpy + queueing for fallback path to decouple host stalls from kernel handoff timing.
- Instrument fused-op backend with register-pressure estimator and, if above threshold, switch to a conservative op order.

Open questions / anomalies:
- Why do some prefetch->fallback events not show corresponding memcpy peaks? Possible explanation: the fallback was decided on kernel heuristic without host memcpy but still causes kernel-level register pressure that blocks subsequent kernels. Need deeper per-kernel SM trace.
- Are there interactions with NVLink peer-to-peer traffic in dedicated clusters? We saw a few spikes only when co-located jobs had cross-GPU comms.
- Quantization mode seemed to change behavior (int8 path showed more severe tails). Is this due to differing kernel code paths or larger memory working sets?

Next experiments (planned):
- Capture CUPTI per-kernel metrics for fallback windows to see SM occupancy and local memory usage.
- Run deterministic microbench with re-played trace but with kernel-priming fast-path injected to measure tail reduction.
- A/B test cooldown hysteresis vs asynchronous memcpy on a canary fleet of 3 nodes.
- Engage infra to reproduce on multi-GPU NVLink topology and isolate peer-to-peer noise.

Notes-to-self / TODOs: 
- Create a focused replay harness (single-file script) that emits rps-client config + seed so others can reproduce locally.
- Open a short-lived reprioritized ticket (SRV-1291) to add kernel-priming fast-path prototype.
- Add a small e2e telemetry field in our trace contract: kernel_handoff_id so downstream systems can attribute tails to a single handoff event.

References & artifacts:
- PR 842: experimental kernel-switch logs and prefetch knobs (linked above).
- Slack thread: #attn-jitter (link above).
- Benchmark scripts: gist link (TODO: upload to repo).

Appendix: raw anecdotal log excerpt (sanitized)
[2024-12-03T19:14:11Z] req=24321 seq=short kernel_choice=flash -> ok latency=34ms
[2024-12-03T19:14:12Z] req=24322 seq=long kernel_choice=flash priming=true memcpy=6.8ms kernel_lat=312ms spike
[2024-12-03T19:14:12Z] req=24323 seq=short kernel_choice=paged memcpy=0.9ms kernel_lat=29ms

If you're poking at this please drop notes inline here or ping me/kenji in slack. I'm planning a concise runbook once we confirm that priming fast-path reduces P99 by ~40% in the toy model.

-- maya
